unit.title: Conversation Lab
unit.summary: Practice real-world pickleball conversations: game recaps, line calls, gear talk, watching together, ratings, fandom, invitations and say-this lines.

lessons.title: After her league night
lessons.objective: Respond with curiosity to a play recap without offering unasked-for advice.

payload.title: She beat the tougher team
payload.setting: Sam texts after her team finally took a game off a stronger pair.

exchanges.theirMessage: Guess who finally beat the 4.0 pair tonight? Us! I'm still buzzing.

replies.text: No way! What clicked for you two?
replies.theirResponse: We stopped trying to bang it and just out-dinked them. Patience paid off.
replies.coachNote: You celebrated and asked a real question.

replies.text: Congrats!! That's awesome.
replies.theirResponse: Thank you! It felt so good.
replies.coachNote: Warm, but a question would keep her talking.

replies.text: They probably weren't really that good.
replies.theirResponse: Wow. Okay. They were good.
replies.coachNote: Never shrink her win.

exchanges.theirMessage: My partner held the kitchen line all night. I just kept my dinks low.

replies.text: So low dinks from you and a partner owning the line? Did it feel different from usual?
replies.theirResponse: Totally. I was calm for once, and so were they.
replies.coachNote: Restating what you heard shows you followed.

replies.text: Sounds like a good plan.
replies.theirResponse: It was. We should do it again.
replies.coachNote: Friendly, but it does not go deeper.

replies.text: Must have been luck.
replies.theirResponse: It wasn't luck. We earned it.
replies.coachNote: Do not credit luck over her effort.

payload.closingNote: A dink is a soft, low shot into the opponent's kitchen. When she shares a win, celebrate first and then ask what worked.

statement.speaker: Casey
statement.text: We got pickled in that second game. I was so mad.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Her team lost 11-0, a shutout.
She is upset about one bad point.
They were actually winning but she's being humble.
She's confused about the score.

payload.translation: Pickled means losing a game without scoring a point, usually 11-0. It is one of the hardest losses to take.

followUps.line: Ouch, a shutout is brutal. What happened that game?
followUps.why: Shows you understand the severity and invites the story.

followUps.line: Did it feel like they were just on fire?
followUps.why: Gives her a way to vent without you offering fixes.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Shutout games hurt. Show empathy, and do not minimize it or offer unasked fixes.

payload.prompt: After someone tells you about a rough game, which question is best?

options.text: What's one thing that went wrong, and what do you think you'll work on?
You should have played more aggressively.
Did you lose on purpose to make them feel better?
It's not a big deal, honestly.

explanation.correct: Open-ended questions about what went wrong and what's next show you care and you're listening.
explanation.incorrect: Follow-up questions should be curious and supportive, not dismissive or prescriptive.
explanation.sayThisLine: What went wrong, and what do you want to work on?

pairs.definition: A soft, short shot that lands in the opponent's kitchen near the net.
Losing a game without scoring, usually 11-0; a shutout.
The 7-foot no-volley zone on each side of the net.

explanation.summary: A dink is a soft kitchen shot, pickled means a shutout loss, and the kitchen is the no-volley zone by the net.
explanation.sayThisLine: Dinking in the kitchen is core pickleball. Getting pickled is rough.

lessons.title: The line call story
lessons.objective: Listen to a line-call dispute without taking sides or escalating.

payload.title: She made the close call
payload.setting: Sam is still thinking about a line call she made at open play.

exchanges.theirMessage: I called a ball out today and I wasn't 100% sure. I've been thinking about it all night.

replies.text: That's a tough spot. What do you usually do when you're not sure?
replies.theirResponse: We're supposed to give the other side the benefit of the doubt. I didn't, and I feel bad.
replies.coachNote: Asking how she usually handles it lets her explain the etiquette.

replies.text: Don't worry about it.
replies.theirResponse: Thanks, but I do worry.
replies.coachNote: Kind, but it brushes past what she told you.

replies.text: Everyone blows calls. Forget it.
replies.theirResponse: It matters to me to be fair.
replies.coachNote: Do not dismiss her sense of fairness.

exchanges.theirMessage: I told them I wasn't sure and offered to replay the point.

replies.text: That's a gracious move. How did they react?
replies.theirResponse: They were relieved. We replayed it and the whole game got friendlier.
replies.coachNote: You recognized the good call and asked about it.

replies.text: Nice of you.
replies.theirResponse: Thanks. It felt right.
replies.coachNote: Kind, but a question would land better.

replies.text: You shouldn't have. You'll lose points that way.
replies.theirResponse: It's rec play. Being fair matters more than a point.
replies.coachNote: Open play is about fun and fair play, not squeezing points.

payload.closingNote: Lines are in, and in doubt you give the other side the benefit of the doubt. A fair call is a good story to ask about.

statement.speaker: Quinn
statement.text: Everyone's calling lines so tight today. Half the close ones are going out.

payload.question: What is Quinn talking about?

options.text: Players are calling close balls out more than usual, even though a ball touching the line is good.
The court's lines are faded, so calls are hard to make.
A new rule says lines don't count as in anymore.
The referees are favoring one side.

payload.translation: In pickleball a ball touching any part of a line is in. Quinn feels opponents are calling close balls out more often than they should.

followUps.line: Is it happening on both sides, or mostly one?
followUps.why: A fair question about the pattern without assigning blame.

followUps.line: That sounds frustrating. Does it change how you play close balls?
followUps.why: Shows empathy and invites her to share.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Line calls can be hard to judge. Listen without taking sides.

payload.prompt: When someone complains about a line call, the best response is to:

options.text: Ask how they handled it and show empathy for the frustration.
Tell them they should always appeal to the ref.
Insist that the other player must have cheated.
Say 'it's just a game' and move on.

explanation.correct: Listening and empathizing without assigning blame keeps the relationship strong.
explanation.incorrect: Escalating, dismissing, or assuming cheating does not help. Most open play has no ref to appeal to anyway.
explanation.sayThisLine: That sounds frustrating. How did you handle it?

payload.prompt: In open play, if a ball touches the line, it is out. True?

scene.alt: Disputed line call at open play.

explanation.correct: In pickleball, lines are in. A ball touching any part of a line is good.
explanation.incorrect: The rule is that lines are in. The kitchen line is the usual exception for volleys and serves, but a ball touching the baseline or a sideline is good.
explanation.sayThisLine: When it touches the line, it's in.

lessons.title: The new paddle
lessons.objective: Ask smart gear questions without pretending expertise.

payload.title: Paddle shopping
payload.setting: Sam is trying to pick a new paddle and feeling overwhelmed.

exchanges.theirMessage: I'm shopping for a new paddle and there are a million. Elongated? Standard? Polymer core? Help.

replies.text: That's a lot of choices. What do you want the paddle to do better for you?
replies.theirResponse: More control at the kitchen. I keep popping my dinks up.
replies.coachNote: You asked about her goal instead of guessing at gear.

replies.text: Just get the one with good reviews.
replies.theirResponse: Everything has good reviews, that's the problem.
replies.coachNote: It sounds like help, but it skips what she needs.

replies.text: Buy the most expensive one.
replies.theirResponse: That's not how this works.
replies.coachNote: Price is not fit. Do not play the expert.

exchanges.theirMessage: A friend says I should demo a few before buying.

replies.text: That sounds smart. Do people at your courts let you try theirs?
replies.theirResponse: Yes! A few said I could borrow theirs for a game.
replies.coachNote: You backed her plan and asked a practical question.

replies.text: Yeah, try before you buy.
replies.theirResponse: Right? That's the plan.
replies.coachNote: Agreeable, but a question would help her more.

replies.text: Demoing is a waste of time. Just order online.
replies.theirResponse: I want to actually feel them first.
replies.coachNote: Do not overrule a sensible plan with a hunch.

payload.closingNote: You do not need paddle expertise. Ask what she wants the paddle to do, and back her plan to try a few.

statement.speaker: Blake
statement.text: My new paddle is so gritty. I can put spin on dinks now that I never could before.

payload.question: What does Blake mean?

options.text: The paddle face is textured (rough/gritty), which grips the ball more and makes more spin.
The paddle is dirty and Blake needs to clean it.
The paddle is low quality and falling apart.
The paddle is too hard and hurts Blake's arm.

payload.translation: A rough or textured paddle face grips the ball better, which lets players create more spin.

followUps.line: Does the grit make your dinks dive more?
followUps.why: A curious question about the effect, without pretending to know the science.

followUps.line: Did it take long to get used to?
followUps.why: Invites a story about how the paddle changed her game.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Paddle surface texture is real gear talk. Listen and ask, and do not pretend to know the materials science.

payload.prompt: When someone talks about a new paddle, what's the best question?

options.text: How does it feel? Is it easier to control or hit harder?
Is that the most expensive paddle on the market?
You should have gotten the other brand instead.
Paddle choice is totally personal, nobody agrees anyway.

explanation.correct: Asking about feel and control shows genuine interest in how the gear affects their play.
explanation.incorrect: Generic reactions, dismissing, or prescribing do not engage with what matters to them.
explanation.sayThisLine: How does it feel? Is it easier to control?

payload.prompt: Which paddle face creates more spin?

image.alt: Two paddle faces: one smooth and one textured/gritty.

options.text: Smooth paddle face
Textured/rough paddle face

explanation.correct: A textured face grips the ball better, so it makes more spin.
explanation.incorrect: It is the texture that grips the ball. A smooth face slides more and makes less spin.
explanation.sayThisLine: Gritty grips the ball. Smooth lets it slide.

lessons.title: Watching the finals together
lessons.objective: Follow along with someone watching a match and ask what just happened.

payload.title: The Erne
payload.setting: You and Sam are watching a pro mixed doubles match on a stream.

exchanges.theirMessage: Did you see that?! An Erne! She jumped around the kitchen and put it away.

replies.text: Wait, she went around the kitchen? How is that legal?
replies.theirResponse: She never touched the kitchen. She jumped from outside the sideline and hit it in the air.
replies.coachNote: An honest question about a move you do not know is perfect.

replies.text: Wow, that looked crazy!
replies.theirResponse: Right?! It's such a risky shot.
replies.coachNote: Enthusiastic, but it does not show you followed.

replies.text: Isn't that cheating?
replies.theirResponse: No, it's legal. She just didn't land in the kitchen.
replies.coachNote: Do not jump to cheating. Ask how it works.

exchanges.theirMessage: It only works if she lands outside the kitchen. Timing is everything.

replies.text: So it's high risk? What happens if she lands in it?
replies.theirResponse: If she lands in the kitchen after the volley, it's a fault. That's why it's so bold.
replies.coachNote: A good question that shows you grasped the key rule.

replies.text: Makes sense.
replies.theirResponse: It's hard to explain without seeing it.
replies.coachNote: Friendly, but it misses a chance to learn.

replies.text: Looks easy enough. I could do that.
replies.theirResponse: Ha. Go ahead and try it.
replies.coachNote: Do not claim you could do what pros just did.

payload.closingNote: An Erne is a volley hit from outside the kitchen after jumping around it. Ask how it works and let her explain.

statement.speaker: Taylor
statement.text: Did you see that dink rally? Someone finally popped one up and it was over.

payload.question: What is Taylor describing?

options.text: A long soft rally where one player hit too high, the opponent attacked and won.
A player served and the return went over the net.
A player got lucky and hit a random shot that worked.
A player reset the ball and they started over.

payload.translation: In a dink rally (soft kitchen shots), the first player to hit the ball too high, or pop it up, usually loses the point because the opponent can attack it.

followUps.line: Who had the better placement in that rally?
followUps.why: Shows you are following the strategy, not just the result.

followUps.line: How long did the dink rally go?
followUps.why: A curious question that lets her relive the rally.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Dink rallies are the heart of pickleball. Watch for the pattern: patience wins until someone pops it up.

payload.prompt: While watching a pro match, what helps you follow along?

options.text: Asking your person 'what just happened?' and listening to their explanation.
Pretending you understand everything and nodding along silently.
Criticizing the players' shots.
Checking your phone instead of watching.

explanation.correct: Asking honest questions and listening to their explanations is the best way to learn and bond.
explanation.incorrect: Pretending, criticizing or ignoring all miss the chance to connect.
explanation.sayThisLine: What just happened there? I'd love the explanation.

payload.prompt: In a dink rally, whoever hits the ball hardest usually wins the point. True?

scene.alt: A long dink rally at the kitchen.

explanation.correct: Dink rallies are usually won by patience, precision and soft placement, not power.
explanation.incorrect: In a dink rally, hitting hard at a low ball tends to pop up or net. The player who stays patient and accurate usually wins.
explanation.sayThisLine: In a dink rally, the patient player usually wins.

lessons.title: Rating talk
lessons.objective: Handle conversations about skill levels and DUPR without fake confidence.

payload.title: Her rating dipped
payload.setting: Sam is down about a recent drop in her DUPR.

exchanges.theirMessage: My DUPR went down after this weekend. I'm kind of sulking about it.

replies.text: Ugh, that's a bummer. What happened in those matches?
replies.theirResponse: I lost to a couple of lower-rated players. That's what stings.
replies.coachNote: You empathized first and then asked about the matches.

replies.text: It's just a number. Don't worry about it.
replies.theirResponse: It matters to me, though.
replies.coachNote: Do not shrink something she cares about.

replies.text: Maybe you're not as good as you thought.
replies.theirResponse: Wow. Okay. Thanks.
replies.coachNote: Never attack her confidence.

exchanges.theirMessage: Everyone says don't stress over ratings. But I do.

replies.text: What would feel like a win for you this month?
replies.theirResponse: Honestly, playing relaxed and finishing three matches without getting tight.
replies.coachNote: Asking for her own goal is supportive and non-judgmental.

replies.text: Yeah, that makes sense.
replies.theirResponse: Thanks for getting it.
replies.coachNote: Kind, but it does not go further.

replies.text: You should just play more tournaments.
replies.theirResponse: I didn't ask for a training plan.
replies.coachNote: Unasked advice lands badly.

payload.closingNote: Ratings can feel personal. Ask what happened and what she wants from her game, and do not hand out advice.

statement.speaker: Jordan
statement.text: Everyone in that bracket was sandbagging. These 3.5s were playing 4.0 level.

payload.question: What does Jordan mean?

options.text: Players were rated lower than their actual skill to get an advantage in brackets.
The players were exhausted and playing poorly.
The players were helping each other win.
Nobody understood the rating system.

payload.translation: Sandbagging is entering a lower division than your real level to win more easily. Jordan is saying the bracket was not fair.

followUps.line: That sounds frustrating. Do you think it was on purpose?
followUps.why: Invites her view without you becoming the judge.

followUps.line: Did you feel outmatched, or were the games close?
followUps.why: Keeps the conversation on her experience.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You cannot know whether someone sandbagged. Listen to her frustration without accusing anyone.

payload.prompt: When someone says they're a 3.5 trying to reach 4.0, what's the best response?

options.text: Ask what the main challenge is for that jump.
Tell them you're already a 5.0.
Say that ratings don't matter.
Suggest they're probably overrated.

explanation.correct: Asking about the challenge shows interest in their goals and progress.
explanation.incorrect: Bragging, dismissing or doubting all miss the point of the conversation.
explanation.sayThisLine: What's the main thing standing between you and 4.0?

pairs.definition: A player's skill level on a scale from about 2.5 to 5.0+; often used to place players in brackets.
Dynamic Universal Pickleball Rating; a system that tracks skill based on match results.
Playing or rating below your true skill level to compete in an easier bracket.

explanation.summary: A rating is a level, DUPR follows match results, and sandbagging is entering below your true level.
explanation.sayThisLine: A rating is where you stand. DUPR follows your results.

lessons.title: Her team lost
lessons.objective: Support an MLP fan after a heartbreaking loss without dismissing fandom.

payload.title: Season over
payload.setting: Sam's MLP team was just knocked out of the playoffs.

exchanges.theirMessage: We're out. The season's over. I'm not even sure what to do with my weekend.

replies.text: I'm so sorry. What's the moment you'll remember from this season?
replies.theirResponse: The home opener. The crowd was unreal, and we won.
replies.coachNote: You acknowledged the loss and invited a happier memory.

replies.text: There's always next season.
replies.theirResponse: I know. It just stings today.
replies.coachNote: True, but too soon. Let her feel it first.

replies.text: Whatever, it's only pickleball.
replies.theirResponse: It's not only pickleball to me.
replies.coachNote: Never shrink her fandom.

exchanges.theirMessage: I'm already checking the roster news for next year.

replies.text: Already? Who are you hoping they pick up?
replies.theirResponse: A strong mixed player, honestly. That's where we lost games.
replies.coachNote: You matched her forward-looking mood with a question.

replies.text: Sounds exhausting.
replies.theirResponse: It's fun for me.
replies.coachNote: Not mean, but it misses her excitement.

replies.text: Maybe try a new hobby.
replies.theirResponse: Pickleball is my hobby.
replies.coachNote: Do not tell her to care less.

payload.closingNote: After a loss, sympathize first, then let her steer to memories or next season. Never tell a fan to care less.

statement.speaker: Morgan
statement.text: My team's roster is so strong on paper but we keep dropping matches we should win.

payload.question: What is Morgan talking about?

options.text: The team has strong players but isn't winning as much as expected.
The roster isn't actually good and Morgan is overestimating them.
The league is rigging results against the team.
There's a problem with the team roster on official documents.

payload.translation: 'On paper' means in theory. The team looks strong, but its real results do not match that.

followUps.line: Is it the mixed games where they slip, or something else?
followUps.why: Engages with the analysis she is already doing.

followUps.line: That's frustrating when the roster looks so good. What do you think is missing?
followUps.why: Invites her view instead of offering a theory.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Teams have ups and downs from pressure, fit and form. Ask what she thinks is behind it.

payload.prompt: After her favorite team loses, what helps most?

options.text: Show empathy, acknowledge the loss hurt, remind her the season continues.
Tell her to stop being so emotionally invested.
Point out the team's weaknesses and why they deserved to lose.
Suggest she root for a better team instead.

explanation.correct: Empathy, validation and perspective help a fan through disappointment.
explanation.incorrect: Dismissing, criticizing or mocking all drive people away.
explanation.sayThisLine: That's rough. I know how much that team means to you.

payload.prompt: Your person just texted that their MLP team lost and they're devastated. What do you do?

situation.narrative: She's passionate about her team. A loss hurts.

facts.label: What she said
facts.value: We just lost a crucial playoff-positioning game.

options.label: Reach out and ask what happened; listen
options.consequence: Perfect. You show you care and create space for her to process.

options.label: Send a quick 'sorry' and nothing else
options.consequence: Kind, but she may want to talk about it, and a one-word reply closes the door.

options.label: Ignore it and change the subject later
options.consequence: She'll feel unsupported and alone in her disappointment.
considerations: You miss a moment to connect

payload.expertNote: MLP fans live and die with their teams. A supportive text means everything after a tough loss.

lessons.title: "You should come play"
lessons.objective: Accept an invitation to play honestly, admitting what you don't know.

payload.title: The beginner clinic
payload.setting: Sam invites you to a beginner clinic on Sunday morning.

exchanges.theirMessage: There's a beginner clinic Sunday at 10. Want to try it with me?

replies.text: Yes! I've never held a paddle, so a clinic sounds perfect.
replies.theirResponse: Perfect. They lend paddles, so just bring water and sneakers.
replies.coachNote: Honest about your level and enthusiastic.

replies.text: Maybe, let me check my schedule.
replies.theirResponse: Sure, let me know.
replies.coachNote: Fine, but a yes would make her day.

replies.text: I'm sure I'd be better than most beginners.
replies.theirResponse: Ha. We'll see about that.
replies.coachNote: Do not brag before you have held a paddle.

exchanges.theirMessage: I want to teach you the kitchen rule first. It trips everyone up.

replies.text: Teach me! I thought we couldn't step in there at all.
replies.theirResponse: You can! You just can't volley while you're standing in it.
replies.coachNote: Admitting a misconception invites her to teach you.

replies.text: Sure, whatever you think.
replies.theirResponse: Okay, I'll explain at the courts.
replies.coachNote: Polite, but you could show curiosity.

replies.text: I already know it. You can't step in the kitchen.
replies.theirResponse: Actually, you can. You just can't volley in it.
replies.coachNote: Pretending to know it while wrong is the worst combination.

payload.closingNote: Being honest about your level is braver and kinder than faking. Say yes, admit what you do not know, and let her teach you.

payload.prompt: You're invited to play but worried you'll embarrass yourself. What do you say?

situation.narrative: She wants you to join. You're nervous.

facts.label: What you feel
facts.value: Anxious about being the worst player.

options.label: Say yes, be honest about nerves, ask what to expect
options.consequence: Honest acceptance with real questions builds connection and sets expectations.

options.label: Politely say no to avoid looking bad
options.consequence: It avoids the nerves, but it also skips the chance to bond over something she loves.

options.label: Say yes and pretend you're experienced
options.consequence: She'll notice immediately during play and feel misled.
considerations: Gets exposed in the first rally

payload.expertNote: Honesty about your level is attractive. Faking it is the opposite.

statement.speaker: Devon
statement.text: I'm still learning the kitchen rule. It's confusing.

payload.question: What is Devon doing?

options.text: Being honest about not fully understanding a core rule and open to learning.
Admitting they're a bad player and will never improve.
Pretending to learn to impress someone.
Saying they're giving up on pickleball.

payload.translation: Saying 'I'm still learning' or 'I don't understand yet' is strength, not weakness. It opens the door to real connection.

followUps.line: Same here, honestly. Want to figure it out together?
followUps.why: Turns confusion into a shared learning moment.

followUps.line: Which part trips you up the most?
followUps.why: A curious question that lets Devon teach.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Saying 'I'm still learning' builds trust. Pretending you know when you do not destroys it.

payload.prompt: When you don't understand a pickleball concept, what's the best move?

options.text: Say 'I'm still learning that' and ask them to explain.
Nod and pretend you understand.
Change the subject so she doesn't know you're lost.
Tell her she's explaining it wrong.

explanation.correct: Admitting gaps and asking for help is honest and invites her to teach you.
explanation.incorrect: Pretending, dodging or blaming all erode trust.
explanation.sayThisLine: I'm still learning that one. Can you explain it?

lessons.title: Say-this gauntlet
lessons.objective: Decode five real fan and player lines in quick succession.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: That was a total pop-up. Free smash.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: A weak, high ball that the opponent could attack easily.
A serve that clipped the net.
A lucky shot that went in.
A deep lob over everyone's head.

payload.translation: A pop-up is a soft shot that floats up high enough to be smashed. 'Free smash' means the other team got an easy put-away.

followUps.line: Who popped it up, and did they get punished?
followUps.why: A follow-up that shows you understood.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You only need to recognize the line. Ask what happened next.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: I got caught in transition all night.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: She kept getting stuck in the middle of the court, between the baseline and the kitchen line.
She had a hard time getting to the courts.
She was stuck inside the kitchen.
She kept changing partners.

payload.translation: The transition zone is the middle of the court. Getting caught there means you are too far up to defend deep balls and too far back to attack, so players try to move through it quickly.

followUps.line: Were they hitting at your feet?
followUps.why: Shows you know why the middle is hard.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need the footwork details. Ask what made it hard.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: We're stacking on the next point.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: She and her partner will line up so each ends up on the side they prefer.
They're putting their paddles in the queue.
They're switching to rally scoring.
They're taking a break.

payload.translation: Stacking is a formation trick in doubles: partners arrange their starting positions so each one gets to play their preferred side. It is not the paddle stack at open play.

followUps.line: Is that so you each get your forehand in the middle?
followUps.why: A guess framed as a question, not a claim.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Stacking is easy to confuse with the paddle stack. If you are unsure which she means, ask.

statement.speaker: Sam
statement.text: He stepped in the kitchen on that volley. Fault.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: He hit the ball in the air while touching the kitchen, which is a fault.
He is never allowed to enter the kitchen.
His serve landed in the kitchen.
He touched the net.

payload.translation: You can stand in the kitchen, but you cannot volley while touching it. Volleying from there, or touching its line, is a fault.

followUps.line: Did anyone call it, or did they keep playing?
followUps.why: A curious question about what happened.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The kitchen rule is about volleying, not standing. Do not claim more detail than you know.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: Her team has 4, the other team has 2, and she is the first server.
It is 4:21 on the clock.
The game is being played to 4.
Four players, two courts, one referee.

payload.translation: In doubles the score is called as serving score, receiving score, then server number. So 4-2-1 means the serving team has 4, the other team has 2, and the first server is serving.

followUps.why: Shows you can read a three-number score.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Three-number scores are a doubles thing. If you lose the thread, ask what the last number means.

payload.prompt: After hearing any of these lines, what's your reflex move?

options.text: Ask a curious follow-up that shows you understood the line.
Change the subject.
Offer unsolicited advice about what they should do.
Repeat the line back as if you said it.

explanation.correct: A follow-up question shows you got it and care about the story.
explanation.incorrect: Dodging, advising or faking all kill the conversation flow.
explanation.sayThisLine: Oh nice, tell me what happened next.

payload.prompt: If she says 'I'm a 3.5,' you know exactly how every shot of hers will look. True?

choices.label: False, it's only a rough guide

explanation.correct: Right. A rating is a useful rough guide to her level, but it does not describe her strengths, her weak spots or her style.
explanation.incorrect: A rating gives you a general level, not a shot-by-shot picture. Two 3.5 players can look very different.
explanation.sayThisLine: What's the part of your game you like best at 3.5?

pairs.definition: Soft kitchen shot; the foundation of pickleball.
Whether the ball is in or out; self-officiated in open play.

distractorDefinitions: An ancient name for the game

explanation.summary: A dink is a soft shot, pickled means a shutout, and a line call is the in-or-out judgment.
explanation.sayThisLine: You now understand the core conversation vocabulary. You're in.
